lesson.title: The Loop's Own Else: When 'else' Means 'Never Broke'
lesson.summary: Python lets you attach an else block to a for loop or while loop; that block runs only if the loop finished normally, without ever hitting a break statement.
lesson.body:
Python has a piece of syntax that surprises almost everyone the first time they see it: for loops and while loops can have their own else clause, written at the same indentation level as the loop itself. It does not mean 'otherwise' the way an else attached to an if statement does. A loop's else block runs when the loop finishes on its own, by exhausting a sequence or by its condition becoming false, and it is skipped entirely if the loop was cut short by a break statement. In other words, else here means 'the loop completed without breaking.'

This only makes sense once you already understand for loops, while loops, and break, because the else clause is defined entirely in terms of how the loop ends. If there is no break anywhere in the loop body, the else block is essentially guaranteed to run every time, which is why the pattern is most useful in loops that search for something and use break the moment they find it. The else clause becomes the natural home for the code that should run only when the search comes up empty.

Here is a search for a target number in a list, using loop-else instead of a separate flag variable:

numbers = [10, 15, 22, 33]
target = 7
for n in numbers:
    if n == target:
        print("Found it")
        break
else:
    print("Not found")

Trace it. The loop checks 10, 15, 22, and 33 against target, which is 7. None of them match, so the if block and its break never execute, and the loop runs to completion normally after checking every element. Because the loop finished without ever calling break, the else block executes, and the program prints Not found. If target had instead been 22, the loop would have printed Found it and immediately broken out, and the else block would have been skipped entirely.

It helps to compare this directly to the flag variable pattern from the previous section. Without loop-else, the same search would need a found flag initialized to False before the loop, set to True inside the if block, and then checked with a separate if statement after the loop ends to decide whether to print Not found. The loop-else clause folds that bookkeeping into the loop's own syntax: no extra variable to initialize, no extra condition to check afterward, and no risk of forgetting to reset the flag if the same loop runs again later in the program.

The same rule applies to while loops. A while loop's else block runs when the loop's condition becomes False on its own, and is skipped if a break exits the loop early. Because the behavior is easy to misread as 'run this if the loop did not execute' or 'run this as the alternative to the loop,' many experienced Python programmers still avoid it in production code and prefer an explicit flag, but recognizing what it means when reading someone else's code, especially in search-and-verify situations, is an essential skill.
